researched_by: the council's own off-street parking places order on the Traffic Penalty Tribunal register, its published car park and campervan guidance, its PSPO pages, and the 2016 and 2022 committee papers in which it decided not to provide
policy_summary:
TORBAY IS THE MIRROR IMAGE OF DEVON COUNTY COUNCIL, AND IT IS THE CLEANEST EXAMPLE IN THE DATASET OF AN AUTHORITY THAT PROHIBITS SLEEPING RATHER THAN PARKING. Torbay has been a unitary authority since 1 April 1998 and is not part of Devon County Council's area; nothing in the Devon file applies here. Because it is unitary it owns both sides of the problem - the highway and 46 car parks with over 7,500 spaces - and it has used only one of them.

THE OPERATIVE INSTRUMENT IS ARTICLE 24 OF THE BOROUGH OF TORBAY (OFF STREET PARKING PLACES) ORDER. The wording is short and absolute: 'No person shall use any part of a parking place or any vehicle left in a parking place - (1) for sleeping or camping purposes; (2) for heating cooking or preparing food'. It applies to every council car park, all year, at every hour, to every vehicle. It is not a motorhome rule and it does not mention motor caravans, campervans or overnight parking anywhere. It catches a car camper and a converted panel van exactly as it catches a coachbuilt motorhome, because it bites on the ACT, not the vehicle. Compare Devon County Council's Schedule 14, which bans the WAITING of a DVLA-bodied motor caravan on two seafronts and creates no offence of sleeping at all. Devon regulates the body type on the highway; Torbay regulates the behaviour in the car park. A van that is legal in Exmouth for the wrong reason is illegal in Torquay for the right one, and vice versa.

ARTICLE 5 SAYS MOTORHOMES ARE WELCOME - TO PARK. The same order designates parking places for 'motor cars, commercial vehicles, coaches, motorcycles, motor homes, pedal cycles or disabled persons vehicles'. Motor homes are an expressly named permitted class. So the regime is: park yes, sleep no. The council's own guidance states both halves on one page - 'Campervans and motor homes are welcome on our car parks where we do not have height barriers installed' and 'Overnight sleeping in vehicles or camping is not permitted, nor is the heating, cooking or preparing of food.'

THE PRACTICAL GATE IS PHYSICAL, NOT LEGAL. Torbay publishes a list of 21 car parks open to campervans and motorhomes, and the criterion is simply the absence of a height barrier. TORQUAY: Abbey Park, Brunswick Square, Chilcote Close, Hampton Avenue, Lymington Road, Meadfoot Beach, Melville Street, Princes Street, Sheddon Hill, St Marychurch, Town Hall, Walls Hill. PAIGNTON: Churchward Road, Clennon Valley, Colin Road, Preston Gardens, Station Lane, Youngs Park. BRIXHAM: Breakwater, Freshwater, Oxen Cove. The two biggest beach car parks in Paignton are deliberately not on it: Broadsands has a 1.98m barrier over 575 spaces and Goodrington 1.9m. At the pressure points the exclusion is a steel bar, not an order.

THE CHARGING CLOCK LEAVES A REAL GAP. Charges run 07:00 to midnight. The longest ticket sold anywhere in Torbay is 'up to 17 hours' (GBP9.90 to GBP11.30 depending on zone) - there is no 24-hour tariff and no overnight product. What Torbay calls an 'overnight' tariff, GBP5.00 to GBP5.20, is only sold at short-stay car parks and only covers 18:00 to midnight. From midnight to 07:00 nothing is chargeable. So in a 24-hour, no-barrier car park such as Preston Gardens, Meadfoot Beach, Abbey Park, Freshwater, Oxen Cove or Berry Head, a motorhome can stand overnight lawfully and free between midnight and 07:00 - it just cannot be slept in. That is the whole of Torbay's overnight regime, and it is why the council never needed a no-overnight-parking order.

ON-STREET, TORBAY HAS DONE NOTHING AT ALL, AND SAYS SO IN WRITING. Six on-street orders are active - the Torquay, Paignton and Brixham consolidated waiting orders 2026, the Street Parking Places (Pay and Display) Order 2026 and the CPZ and Resident Permit Parking Places Consolidation Order 2025. No motor-caravan prohibition, no overnight waiting ban and no seafront vehicle-class restriction was found in any of them, and none of the council's proposed-TRO pages for Torquay, Paignton or Brixham carries one. The November 2022 officer appraisal states the council's legal position bluntly: 'it is not an offence to use a vehicle on the highway for eating, sleeping, etc', and the only offence available is that 'it is an offence to discharge effluent or waste on to the highway'. Torbay's actual on-street constraint is ordinary residential parking control - five controlled parking zones (Torquay Harbour North, Brixham Glenmore/Parkham, Preston, Ellacombe and Shiphay) plus pay-and-display on the seafront roads.

THERE IS NO PROVISION, AND THE REFUSAL IS DOCUMENTED AND DELIBERATE. Torbay has no aire, no motorhome bays, no self-containment scheme, no waste or chemical disposal point and no overnight permit. It has considered provision twice and declined twice. In November 2016 the Elected Mayor commissioned consultation on byelaws and traffic regulation orders covering motor homes in residential areas; nothing was ever made. In February 2022 the Transport and Parking Working Party asked officers to look again, and in November 2022 the resulting 'Options Appraisal on a bay wide approach for Motorhome/Campervan Parking' recommended the status quo in terms: 'the existing arrangements should be kept i.e. no overnight parking of motorhomes/campervans in Council car parks', reasoning that 'Torbay does not have the luxury of under capacity in off-street car parking during the summer months' and that users should be directed to existing commercial sites. Option 4.3.1, a feasibility study into overnight provision, was expressly 'not recommended by officers'. Nothing has changed since.

BERRY HEAD IS NOW A COUNCIL CAR PARK, WHICH IS THE BIGGEST CHANGE OF 2026. Berry Head is a country park, National Nature Reserve and SSSI owned by Torbay Council but leased since 1999, with the car park and toilets added by a further lease in December 2017, to the Torbay Coast and Countryside Trust, which enforced parking through private operators. The Trust went into liquidation, and the council took its six sites in-house: Berry Head, Anstey's Cove, Cockington Court, Cockington Cycle Hub, Higher Lodge and Sharkham. Off Street Parking Places Amendment Order No.1 2026, advertised 30 April 2026 and effective 1 May 2026, brought them into the council's own off-street order; former Trust permits stopped being accepted on 3 May 2026 and a GBP85 annual countryside permit replaced them. The consequence for van users is that Article 24 now applies at Berry Head where a private landowner's terms applied before, on top of the Berry Head and Hopes Nose PSPO which has banned camping outright since 1 April 2025.
notes:
The single most useful thing here is the contrast with Devon County Council, and it should be read as a pair. Two adjacent authorities, the same coast, the same vehicles, opposite instruments. Devon wrote a vehicle-class schedule that prohibits a DVLA motor caravan from WAITING on named lengths of Exmouth and Dartmouth highway, and created no sleeping offence anywhere. Torbay wrote a behaviour clause that prohibits SLEEPING in any council car park, and created no motorhome offence anywhere. The practical results are almost inverted: in Devon you may sleep where you may lawfully park, and there are two towns where a motorhome may not park at all; in Torbay a motorhome may park anywhere it physically fits, including free from midnight to 07:00, and may not be slept in anywhere the council owns. Neither council's website tells you this, and a van user driving from Exmouth to Torquay crosses an invisible line where the rule changes shape entirely.

Direction of travel: static, and consciously so. This is not an authority that is tightening - it has made no new restriction against motorhomes since at least 2016 - but it is emphatically not expanding either. It has said no to provision twice, in 2016 and again in the November 2022 options appraisal, and the stated reason is capacity rather than principle: the car parks are full in summer, so there is nothing to give. That reasoning will not change, which makes Torbay one of the least likely English coastal authorities to open an aire. Set it against South Ayrshire, which built provision because it had a pollution problem, and against East Devon, which absorbed the vehicles Devon CC pushed off the Exmouth seafront. Torbay has neither pressure valve: it displaces nothing onto anyone, and it provides nothing.

Enforcement reality is the weak point of the whole regime and a human should treat it with care. Article 24 is a prohibition in a parking places order, not one of the standard civil enforcement contraventions, and no penalty charge code for 'sleeping in a vehicle' was found. The order's own remedy for breach sits in Articles 29 and 30 - authorised officers may remove or reposition a vehicle and recover the cost as a civil debt. In practice this means a knock on the window rather than a ticket, and the reports of van users bear that out. A motorhome that pays for its bay, keeps its blinds down and moves on early is very unlikely to meet enforcement; the clause exists to give officers something to point at when there is a complaint. Torbay's parking enforcement effort is aimed at the thing it can actually ticket, which is a vehicle overhanging its bay - the guidance warns twice that a motorhome occupying more than one bay must buy a ticket for each and that overhanging vehicles get a PCN.

Berry Head was worth checking before recording and the answer changed during 2026. Until this year it was not a council car park in any operational sense - Torbay owned the freehold but the Torbay Coast and Countryside Trust held the lease and used private operators (Premier Park, later Park with Ease) with ANPR, and there is an FOI trail disputing the validity of notices issued while the lease position was unclear. The Trust's liquidation reversed that. Anyone re-checking this file should confirm the amendment order actually landed, because the transition is only weeks old.

Torbay also has byelaws prohibiting overnight camping on some open spaces, Churston Common among them, which it describes on its unauthorised encampments page as expensive and slow to enforce. That page is unusually candid, and it explicitly names 'van dwellers' alongside tent dwellers and Gypsy and Traveller communities - the council distinguishes touring vehicles, long-term residence and vehicle storage as three different problems needing three different answers, and has an answer for none of them. It also rejected a pre-emptive borough-wide injunction as costing GBP5,000 to GBP20,000-plus and being useless until an encampment already exists.

One caution on the PSPOs. The Berry Head and Hopes Nose order bans camping and tents by persons; it says nothing about vehicles. It should not be read as a vehicle sleeping ban in its own right - at Berry Head the vehicle prohibition comes from Article 24, and only since May 2026. Torbay's other PSPOs, alcohol across all three towns and dispersal in Torquay town centre, both from 1 May 2024, contain no camping or vehicle content at all.
open_questions: The verbatim text of Articles 5 and 24 was read from the Borough of Torbay (Off Street Parking Places) Order 2025 (made 26 March 2025, in force 24 April 2025). The 2026 order (in force 23 April 2026) is now the operative one, and its PDF on the Traffic Penalty Tribunal register could not be retrieved - the host returned robots.txt refusals on every on-street and 2026 document tried. The council's live guidance repeats the Article 24 wording verbatim, so it plainly carries forward, but the 2026 article numbering has not been confirmed.

The three consolidated on-street orders (Torquay, Paignton and Brixham 2026) were NOT read in full, for the same reason. The conclusion that Torbay has no on-street motor-caravan or overnight prohibition rests on the absence of any such order in the council's TRO listings, the absence of any mention in committee papers, and the council's own written legal position that sleeping on the highway is not an offence. It is a well-supported negative, not a verified one.

The February 2022 working party minutes refer to 'Battery Gardens, where a TRO prohibited motorhome parking' in Brixham. No such order could be found in any published Torbay TRO list. It may be an officer's loose reference to a general waiting restriction, or it may be a genuine schedule entry buried in the Brixham consolidated order. Worth a look at the signage on Berry Head Road by Battery Gardens.

Whether Article 24 breach is enforced by penalty charge notice at all, or only by the removal power in Articles 29-30. No PCN contravention code for sleeping was found and the council does not publish one.

Whether Off Street Parking Places Amendment Order No.1 2026 (advertised 30 April 2026, effective 1 May 2026) was in fact made and now governs Berry Head, Anstey's Cove, Cockington Court, Cockington Cycle Hub, Higher Lodge and Sharkham. Only the notice was seen, not the made order.

A forum post claims designated motorhome parking in the golf course car park at Brixham park and ride. Brixham park and ride is not in the council's published car park list and no designated motorhome bays appear anywhere in the order or the guidance. Probably a misrecollection, but it is the only claim of provision anywhere in Torbay and should be checked on the ground.

Torre Abbey seafront itself. The beach frontage is on-street pay and display on Torbay Road and Kings Drive rather than a car park; Abbey Park on Belgrave Road is the nearest no-barrier 24-hour council car park. Whether any waiting restriction on Torbay Road bites overnight was not established.
The full list of Torbay open-space byelaws prohibiting overnight camping. Only Churston Common is named on the council's encampments page; the byelaws themselves were not located.

sites.name: All Torbay Council car parks (Article 24 - no sleeping, camping, cooking or heating)
sites.notes: The core of the Torbay regime, and it covers all 46 council car parks and over 7,500 spaces. Article 24 of the Borough of Torbay (Off Street Parking Places) Order: 'No person shall use any part of a parking place or any vehicle left in a parking place - (1) for sleeping or camping purposes; (2) for heating cooking or preparing food'. No hours, no vehicle class, no exceptions. Article 5 of the same order expressly designates parking places for 'motor homes' among the permitted vehicle classes, so PARKING a motorhome is authorised and SLEEPING in it is not. Charges run 07:00 to midnight and the longest ticket sold is 'up to 17 hours' - there is no 24-hour tariff, and the GBP5.00-GBP5.20 'overnight' tariff is an 18:00-to-midnight product sold only at short-stay car parks. Nothing is payable between midnight and 07:00. Enforcement recorded as unknown deliberately: no PCN contravention code for sleeping was found, and the order's stated remedy for an Article 24 breach is removal or repositioning of the vehicle by an authorised officer under Articles 29-30 with costs recoverable as a civil debt. The 21 car parks open to campervans and motorhomes are those without height barriers - Torquay: Abbey Park, Brunswick Square, Chilcote Close, Hampton Avenue, Lymington Road, Meadfoot Beach, Melville Street, Princes Street, Sheddon Hill, St Marychurch, Town Hall, Walls Hill; Paignton: Churchward Road, Clennon Valley, Colin Road, Preston Gardens, Station Lane, Youngs Park; Brixham: Breakwater, Freshwater, Oxen Cove.

sites.name: Berry Head Country Park car park, Brixham
sites.search_hint: Berry Head car park, Gillard Road, Brixham
sites.notes: CHECK WHO RUNS IT - THE ANSWER CHANGED IN MAY 2026. Berry Head is a country park, National Nature Reserve and SSSI on land owned by Torbay Council but leased to the Torbay Coast and Countryside Trust since December 1999, with the car park and toilets added by a further lease on 1 December 2017. The Trust enforced parking privately (Premier Park, then Park with Ease, with ANPR) and an FOI request disputes the validity of notices issued between 2015 and 2017. The Trust went into liquidation and the council took the site in-house; Off Street Parking Places Amendment Order No.1 2026, advertised 30 April 2026 and effective 1 May 2026, brought Berry Head, Anstey's Cove, Cockington Court, Cockington Cycle Hub, Higher Lodge and Sharkham into the council's own off-street order. Former Trust permits ceased to be accepted on 3 May 2026 and a GBP85 annual countryside permit replaced them. So Article 24's sleeping and camping prohibition now applies here where a private landowner's terms applied before. Practically it is one of the more attractive spots in Torbay for a large vehicle: open 24 hours, no height restriction, 76 spaces, Zone 2 pay and display topping out at GBP11.00 for 17 hours, and nothing payable midnight to 07:00. The Berry Head and Hopes Nose PSPO bans camping over the headland on top of this. Confidence medium because the amendment order was seen only as a notice.
sites.geocode_precision: TQ5 9AP postcode centroid at the Berry Head car park, address given by the council as Gillard Road, Brixham

sites.name: Berry Head and Hopes Nose (Public Spaces Protection Order) 2025
sites.notes: In force 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2028 over two separate headlands - Berry Head at Brixham and Hopes Nose at Torquay - so no single coordinate is honest. 'No camping shall be permitted at any time' within the areas edged red, and no person may 'erect a tent, shelter, bivouac or anything of a similar nature'. Fires and barbecues are also banned, along with fishing with more than one rod, taking more than 20 mackerel in 24 hours, littering and removing rock. Breach is a fixed penalty of GBP100 or a fine up to level 3 on summary conviction. IMPORTANT: this order regulates camping by persons and says nothing whatever about vehicles. It should not be cited as a vehicle sleeping ban - at Berry Head that comes from Article 24 of the off-street order, and only since May 2026. Torbay's other PSPOs, alcohol across Torquay, Paignton and Brixham and dispersal in Torquay town centre, both from 1 May 2024, contain no camping or vehicle provisions at all.

sites.name: Broadsands car park, Paignton
sites.search_hint: Broadsands car park, Broadsands Road, Paignton
sites.notes: One of the pressure points, and motorhomes are excluded from it by a steel bar rather than an order. Broadsands is the largest beach car park in Torbay at 575 spaces and carries a 1.98m (6'6") height barrier, so it is not on the council's list of car parks open to campervans and motorhomes. It is also gated - 08:00 to 22:00 in summer and 08:00 to 20:00 in winter - so no vehicle of any kind can stand there overnight. Zone 3 long stay, GBP2.00 for an hour up to GBP11.30 for 17 hours, charges 21 March to 31 October only. applies_to recorded as over_length because the schema has no height category; the limit is a height limit, not a length one. The neighbouring Goodrington car park on Tanners Road has a tighter 1.9m barrier over 14 spaces.
sites.geocode_precision: TQ4 6HX postcode centroid on Broadsands Road, the council's published address for the car park

sites.name: Youngs Park car park, Goodrington Sands, Paignton
sites.search_hint: Youngs Park car park, Tanners Road, Goodrington, Paignton
sites.notes: The Goodrington answer, and it is a gate rather than a rule. Youngs Park is the main Goodrington Sands car park, 124 spaces, no height restriction, and it IS on the council's campervan and motorhome list - but it opens 08:00 to 22:00 in summer and 08:00 to 20:00 in winter, so an overnight stay is physically impossible whatever Article 24 says. Recorded with instrument opening_hours because that, not a prohibition, is what actually stops a van staying. Zone 3 long stay, up to GBP11.30 for 17 hours. Times given are the closed window in summer; in winter the gates shut at 20:00. The small Goodrington car park on the same road (14 spaces, 1.9m barrier) is the only place in Torbay advertising a Zone 3 'overnight' tariff, GBP5.20 for 18:00 to midnight, and a motorhome cannot get under its barrier to use it.
sites.geocode_precision: TQ4 6LP postcode centroid on Tanners Road, the council's published address for Youngs Park

sites.name: Preston Gardens car park, Paignton (Preston Sands)
sites.search_hint: Preston Gardens car park, Old Torquay Road, Paignton
sites.notes: The Preston Sands pressure point. Preston Gardens is open 24 hours, has no height restriction and is on the council's campervan and motorhome list, so a motorhome may lawfully stand here through the night - charges run only 07:00 to midnight and the maximum ticket is 17 hours at GBP9.90 (Zone 1 long stay). What it may not do is be slept in, by Article 24. Small at 35 spaces, of which 9 are 20-minute free shopper bays and 2 disabled, so the practical capacity for a large vehicle is thin. This is the shape of the whole Torbay regime in one car park: permission to park, prohibition on sleeping, and no provision of any kind.
sites.geocode_precision: TQ3 2RA postcode centroid on Old Torquay Road; the car park sits inland of Preston Sands

sites.name: Abbey Park car park, Torquay (Torre Abbey seafront)
sites.search_hint: Abbey Park car park, Belgrave Road, Torquay
sites.notes: The nearest council car park to Torre Abbey Sands that a motorhome can use: 27 spaces on Belgrave Road, open 24 hours, no height restriction, on the campervan and motorhome list, Zone 3 long stay at up to GBP11.30 for 17 hours with nothing payable midnight to 07:00. Article 24 still bans sleeping in it. Note that the Torre Abbey seafront itself is not a council car park - the frontage is on-street pay and display on Torbay Road and Kings Drive, and no overnight or motor-caravan restriction was found on either. Confidence medium on the location rather than the rule: the postcode centroid sits on Belgrave Road a few hundred metres inland of the beach.
sites.geocode_precision: TQ2 5HZ postcode centroid on Belgrave Road, the council's published address for Abbey Park car park

sites.name: Torbay open space byelaws prohibiting overnight camping (Churston Common and others)
sites.notes: Torbay's unauthorised encampments page states that the council 'has byelaws prohibiting overnight camping on some open spaces' and names Churston Common as an example, while conceding that enforcement needs security staff, bailiffs, police presence and welfare assessments and is therefore expensive and slow. The byelaws themselves were not located and the full list of covered open spaces is unknown, hence low confidence. The same page is unusually candid in naming 'van dwellers' alongside tent dwellers and Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities, distinguishes touring use from long-term residence from vehicle storage, and records that the council rejected a pre-emptive borough-wide injunction as costing GBP5,000 to GBP20,000-plus and being ineffective until an encampment is already established. Off the highway and outside the car parks, this and section 77-78 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 are what Torbay actually reaches for.
